title: 04. BM25 & Lexical Search: Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) — How Rare a Word Is
summary: Imagine you're an art detective trying to figure out which artist painted a mystery painting by looking at the colours used. > > - Blue is used by every artist in the 18th century.

sections.title: ① Real-World Analogy
sections.body:
> Imagine you're an art detective trying to figure out **which artist painted a mystery painting** by looking at the colours used.
>
> - **Blue** is used by *every artist* in the 18th century. Finding blue tells you nothing.
> - **A very specific shade of burnt sienna mixed with turpentine** is only used by one artist. Finding this colour tells you *everything*.
>
> In search, **"the"** is like blue — it appears everywhere and tells you nothing about relevance. **"Elasticsearch"** is like the rare colour — it only appears in very specific documents, and its presence is highly informative.
>
> **IDF measures how rare and informative a word is.**

sections.title: ② Plain English Explanation
sections.body:
IDF asks: **"How many documents contain this word?"**

- If a word appears in *all* documents → IDF is near 0 (tells us nothing, useless for distinguishing)
- If a word appears in *few* documents → IDF is high (this word is rare and informative)

IDF is calculated across the *entire collection* of documents (not per document like TF). It's a single number per word, shared across all queries.

sections.title: ③ Why Does This Matter?
sections.body:
**Problem:** The word "the" might appear 50 times in a document, giving it a sky-high TF. But "the" appears in *every* document, so it's useless for finding relevant documents.

**Solution:** Weight each word by how *rare* it is across all documents. Rare words are informative; common words are not. IDF provides this weight.

sections.title: ④ Step-by-Step Technical Explanation
sections.body:
**IDF Formula (standard):**

```
IDF(term) = log( N / df(term) )
```

Where:
- `N` = total number of documents in the collection
- `df(term)` = number of documents that contain this term (document frequency)
- `log` = natural logarithm (dampens the effect)

**Numerical Examples (N = 5 documents):**

```
Word "and"     → appears in 4 docs → IDF = log(5/4) = log(1.25) = 0.22  ← LOW (common)
Word "python"  → appears in 3 docs → IDF = log(5/3) = log(1.67) = 0.51  ← MEDIUM
Word "java"    → appears in 2 docs → IDF = log(5/2) = log(2.50) = 0.92  ← MEDIUM-HIGH
Word "enterprise"→ appears in 1 doc → IDF = log(5/1) = log(5.00) = 1.61 ← HIGH (rare!)
Word "great"   → appears in 1 doc → IDF = log(5/1) = log(5.00) = 1.61  ← HIGH
```

> 💡 **The aha moment:** "enterprise" and "great" get high IDF because they're rare. "and" gets near-zero IDF because it's everywhere. This automatically handles stopwords!

**BM25's IDF Formula (slightly different):**
```
IDF_BM25(term) = log( (N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5) + 1 )
```
The `+0.5` prevents division by zero and handles edge cases. We'll use this in Lesson 7.

sections.title: ⑤ Beginner-Friendly Code Example
sections.body:
```python
# ============================================================
# LESSON 4: Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)
# ============================================================

import math
import string

# Our 5 documents (same as before!)
documents = [
    "Python is great for machine learning and data science",
    "Java is used for enterprise software development",
    "Python and Java are both popular programming languages",
    "Machine learning requires lots of data and computation",
    "Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling"
]

def tokenise(text):
    text = text.lower()
    text = text.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))
    return text.split()

tokenised_docs = [tokenise(doc) for doc in documents]

# ── STEP 1: Count how many documents contain each word ────────────────

# N = total number of documents
N = len(documents)
print(f"Total documents (N) = {N}\n")

# Document Frequency: df[word] = number of docs containing word
df = {}
for tokens in tokenised_docs:
    # Use a set to count each word only ONCE per document
    # (even if it appears multiple times in the same doc)
    unique_words_in_doc = set(tokens)
    for word in unique_words_in_doc:
        df[word] = df.get(word, 0) + 1

print("=== Document Frequency (df) ===")
print(f"{'Word':<15} | {'df (# docs with word)':<22} | {'Rarity'}")
print("-" * 60)
for word, count in sorted(df.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True):
    rarity = "common" if count >= 3 else ("medium" if count == 2 else "rare")
    print(f"{word:<15} | {count:<22} | {rarity}")
print()

# ── STEP 2: Compute IDF ───────────────────────────────────────────────

def compute_idf(word, df, N):
    """
    Standard IDF formula: log(N / df(word))
    Higher value = rarer word = more informative
    """
    # df.get(word, 0) handles words not in any document (df=0)
    # We add 1 to df to avoid division by zero (smoothing)
    doc_freq = df.get(word, 0)
    if doc_freq == 0:
        return 0.0  # Word not in any document
    return math.log(N / doc_freq)

# Compute IDF for every unique word
print("=== IDF Values (sorted from highest to lowest) ===")
print(f"{'Word':<15} | {'df':<5} | {'N/df':<8} | {'IDF = log(N/df)':<18} | {'Meaning'}")
print("-" * 75)

all_words = sorted(df.keys())
idf_values = {}
for word in all_words:
    idf = compute_idf(word, df, N)
    idf_values[word] = idf

# Sort by IDF descending to see most informative words first
for word, idf in sorted(idf_values.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True):
    doc_freq = df[word]
    ratio = N / doc_freq
    meaning = "very informative" if idf > 1.2 else ("somewhat useful" if idf > 0.5 else "not very useful")
    print(f"{word:<15} | {doc_freq:<5} | {ratio:<8.2f} | {idf:<18.4f} | {meaning}")

print()

# ── STEP 3: The Key Insight — IDF as a filter ────────────────────────

print("=== IDF in Action: Same count, very different usefulness ===\n")

# Imagine a query: "is python great"
# "is" appears in 2 docs with TF=1 each  → IDF = log(5/2) = 0.916
# "python" appears in 3 docs with TF=1 each → IDF = log(5/3) = 0.511
# "great" appears in 1 doc with TF=1   → IDF = log(5/1) = 1.609

for word in ["is", "python", "great"]:
    idf = idf_values.get(word, 0)
    doc_freq = df.get(word, 0)
    print(f"Word '{word}':")
    print(f"  Appears in {doc_freq} out of {N} documents")
    print(f"  IDF = log({N}/{doc_freq}) = log({N/doc_freq:.2f}) = {idf:.4f}")
    print(f"  → {'Low IDF: this word is common, not very useful for ranking' if idf < 0.7 else 'High IDF: this word is rare and highly informative!'}")
    print()

# ── STEP 4: Visualise IDF as a bar chart (text version) ──────────────

print("=== IDF Bar Chart (each ■ = 0.1 IDF points) ===")
print()
for word in sorted(idf_values.keys()):
    idf = idf_values[word]
    bar_length = int(idf * 10)  # Scale: each ■ = 0.1
    bar = "■" * bar_length
    print(f"  {word:<15} | {bar} {idf:.3f}")
```

sections.title: ⑥ Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
❌ **Mistake 1:** Confusing TF and IDF — thinking IDF is also per-document
✅ **Fix:** IDF is **per-word**, computed across the **entire collection** once. TF is per-document.

❌ **Mistake 2:** Not handling `df = 0` (word not in any document)
✅ **Fix:** Add a check: if `df == 0`, return 0 (or use smoothing like `log((N+1)/(df+1))`)

❌ **Mistake 3:** Thinking low IDF words should be removed entirely
✅ **Fix:** Low IDF words just contribute *less* to the score. Don't remove them — removing stopwords is a separate preprocessing choice.

❌ **Mistake 4:** Confusing document frequency (df) with term frequency (TF)
✅ **Fix:** TF = count within ONE document. DF = number of documents containing the word.

❌ **Mistake 5:** Not recomputing IDF when documents are added
✅ **Fix:** IDF depends on N and df — both change when documents are added. Rebuild IDF when the collection changes.

sections.title: ⑦ Quick Recap
sections.body:
- 🌍 **IDF(word)** = how rare the word is across all documents
- 📐 Formula: `log(N / df(word))` where N = total docs, df = docs containing word
- 📉 Common words ("the", "is", "and") → low IDF → low contribution to score
- 📈 Rare words ("elasticsearch", "quantum") → high IDF → high contribution to score
- 🔄 IDF is computed **once per word** across the entire collection, not per document
